question: What does the declaration "int *ptr;" signify in C/C++?
options: A variable that stores an integer value
A pointer variable that stores the memory address of an integer
explanation: "int *ptr;" declares a pointer variable ptr capable of holding the memory address of an integer data item.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between calloc() and malloc() in the C standard library?
options: malloc() initializes allocated memory to zero; calloc() leaves it uninitialized
calloc() allocates memory and initializes all bytes to zero; malloc() allocates raw uninitialized memory
calloc() allocates stack memory; malloc() allocates heap memory
explanation: calloc(num, size) clears allocated bytes to 0 and takes two arguments; malloc(size) allocates contiguous bytes leaving memory garbage values.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a "Dangling Pointer" in C/C++?
options: A pointer that continues to point to a memory location that has already been deallocated or freed
A pointer that points to another pointer
A pointer stored in read-only memory
explanation: A dangling pointer references deallocated heap memory or out-of-scope stack frames, leading to undefined behavior upon dereference.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a "Memory Leak" in C/C++ program execution?
options: Dynamically allocated heap memory that is no longer needed but has not been freed using free() or delete, wasting available RAM
A physical fault in RAM chips
explanation: Memory leaks occur when pointers to allocated heap blocks are lost without calling free()/delete, depleting system memory over time.
subject: Programming Languages

options: Undefined behavior according to the C standard (modifying a variable more than once between sequence points)
explanation: Modifying a scalar object more than once without an intervening sequence point invokes Undefined Behavior (UB) under the ANSI C standard.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a "Segment Fault" (SIGSEGV) in C/C++?
options: A syntax error detected by the compiler
A runtime error triggered by attempting to access memory that the program does not have permission to access (e.g., dereferencing NULL or out-of-bounds array)
explanation: SIGSEGV occurs when a process attempts to read or write an invalid virtual memory page or violates read-only memory protections.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the purpose of the "static" keyword when applied to a local variable inside a C function?
options: Makes the variable accessible globally across all files
Preserves the variable’s value across repeated function calls by allocating it in the data segment rather than the stack
Prevents the variable from being modified (constant)
Deletes the variable after first execution
explanation: A static local variable retains its value between function invocations because it persists in static data storage for the lifetime of the program.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the role of the "extern" keyword in C/C++?
options: Declares a variable or function that is defined in another translation unit (file) without re-allocating memory for it
explanation: extern informs the compiler that a variable or function exists and has linkage to a definition located in another source file.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the purpose of the "volatile" type qualifier in C/C++?
options: Informs the compiler that an object’s value can change unexpectedly (by hardware or concurrent threads), inhibiting aggressive compiler optimization reads from registers
Speeds up execution by caching in L1
explanation: volatile forces the compiler to reload the variable directly from memory every time it is referenced, crucial for memory-mapped I/O and ISR flags.
subject: Programming Languages

question: In C, what is the fundamental difference between a struct and a union?
options: In a struct, each member has its own separate memory space; in a union, all members share the exact same memory location (sized to its largest member)
Unions can hold functions; structs cannot
explanation: A struct’s total size is the sum of its members (plus padding). A union’s size is determined by its largest member, holding only one member at any given time.
subject: Programming Languages

question: In C++, what is a Reference variable (&ref)?
options: A pointer that can be NULL
An alias (alternative name) for an already existing variable; it must be initialized upon declaration and cannot be reseated
explanation: A C++ reference is an immutable alias to an object; it cannot be NULL, cannot be reseated to another variable, and does not require dereference syntax (*).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is Function Overloading in C++?
options: Defining multiple functions in the same scope with the exact same name but differing parameter lists (types or counts)
Calling a function too many times
Passing infinite arguments to a macro
explanation: Function overloading enables multiple functions to share a name if their signatures (parameter types, order, or arity) differ, resolved at compile-time.
subject: Programming Languages

question: Can a function in C++ be overloaded solely on the basis of different return types?
options: No; overloading resolution depends strictly on parameter lists (the return type alone is insufficient to distinguish calls)
Only if one return type is void
explanation: The compiler cannot deduce which overloaded version to call based purely on return type if argument types are identical.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is an "inline" function in C++?
options: A function that executes on a single line of code
A suggestion to the compiler to substitute the function’s body directly at the call site, eliminating the overhead of a function call
A function running in user space
explanation: Inline functions replace call instructions with expanded code directly at the call site, saving stack frame creation overhead for small functions.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a Copy Constructor in C++ and what is its standard signature for class MyClass?
explanation: A copy constructor creates a new object as a copy of an existing object: MyClass(const MyClass &other); (pass-by-reference is required to prevent infinite recursion).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between Shallow Copy and Deep Copy in C++ when a class encapsulates dynamic memory pointers?
options: Shallow copy duplicates pointer addresses (sharing the same heap memory, leading to double-free errors); deep copy allocates distinct heap memory and copies the actual contents
Shallow copy is slower than deep copy
Deep copy only copies primitive variables
explanation: Default copy constructors perform shallow member-wise copies. Custom copy constructors must allocate new heap memory to execute a safe deep copy.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a Friend Function in C++?
options: A function that can access the private and protected members of a class despite not being a member of that class
A global function that cannot use pointers
explanation: A friend function or friend class is granted explicit access to private and protected attributes of the class declaring it.
subject: Programming Languages

question: In C++, what operator cannot be overloaded?
explanation: Operators that cannot be overloaded in C++ include: scope resolution (::), member selection (.), pointer-to-member (.*), sizeof, and ternary conditional (?:).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What happens when "delete[] ptr;" is called on a dynamic array allocated with "new int[10];"?
options: Only the first element is freed
All destructors (if any) are invoked and the entire block of memory for all array elements is correctly deallocated
explanation: delete[] invokes destructors for each element in the dynamic array and returns the entire allocated memory block back to the heap.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the "Rule of Three" in classic C++ design?
options: If a class defines a Destructor, Copy Constructor, or Copy Assignment Operator, it should almost certainly explicitly define all three
Methods must have at most 3 parameters
explanation: Managing raw dynamic resources requires consistent management across cleanup (destructor), cloning (copy constructor), and reassignment (copy assignment operator).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What are the four foundational pillars of Object-Oriented Programming (OOP)?
explanation: The four core principles of OOP are Encapsulation (data hiding), Abstraction (hiding complexity), Inheritance (code reuse), and Polymorphism (many forms).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is "Encapsulation" in OOP?
options: Allowing all variables to be public
Bundling data (attributes) and methods that operate on that data into a single unit (class) and restricting direct access from the outside (data hiding)
explanation: Encapsulation bundles state and behaviors together while restricting direct access to internal representation using private/protected access modifiers.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is "Abstraction" in OOP?
options: Displaying all implementation details to the user
Hiding background implementation complexities and showing only the essential interfaces/features to the outside world
explanation: Abstraction presents a clean public interface while shielding consumers from underlying internal mechanics (e.g., using abstract classes or interfaces).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is Polymorphism in Object-Oriented Programming?
options: The ability of an entity (function, operator, or object) to take on multiple distinct forms depending on the invocation context
Having multiple subclasses with no methods
Storing multiple types in an array
explanation: Polymorphism enables a single interface to represent different underlying forms, divided into Compile-time (static) and Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is Compile-Time (Static) Polymorphism, and how is it achieved in C++/Java?
options: Method Overloading and Operator Overloading (resolved at compile-time by the compiler)
explanation: Compile-time polymorphism resolves method calls during compilation using parameter signatures (function overloading and operator overloading).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is Run-Time (Dynamic) Polymorphism, and how is it achieved?
options: Method Overriding using Virtual Functions and Dynamic Binding (resolved at runtime based on the actual object type)
explanation: Run-time polymorphism binds function calls dynamically at execution time via virtual methods and virtual function tables (vtables).
subject: Programming Languages

question: In C++, what is a "Pure Virtual Function"?
options: A virtual function with no implementation in the base class, declared with "= 0" (e.g., virtual void draw() = 0;)
A function that takes no parameters
A function that cannot be overridden
explanation: A pure virtual function specifies an abstract interface contract that all derived classes must implement.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is an "Abstract Class"?
options: A class containing at least one pure virtual function (or declared abstract) that CANNOT be directly instantiated into objects
A class that cannot be inherited from
A class with only public members
explanation: Abstract classes define common templates and contracts for subclasses and cannot be instantiated directly with "new" or by value.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the "Diamond Problem" in multiple inheritance, and how is it resolved in C++?
options: A compiler crash; resolved by rebooting

When a subclass inherits from two intermediate classes that both inherit from the same common base class, causing duplicate base class subobjects; resolved using Virtual Inheritance (virtual base classes)
A syntax error with diamond brackets
explanation: Virtual base classes (e.g., class B : virtual public A) ensure that only one shared instance of the ancestor class A is included in the most derived class.
subject: Programming Languages

question: Why should a Base Class Destructor always be declared "virtual" when using polymorphism in C++?
options: To ensure that when a derived object is deleted via a base class pointer, the derived class destructor is invoked properly before the base class destructor, avoiding memory leaks
explanation: If a base class destructor is non-virtual, deleting a derived object via a Base* pointer causes undefined behavior, skipping the derived class destructor.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between Method Overloading and Method Overriding?
options: Overloading occurs within the same class with different parameters (compile-time); Overriding occurs in derived classes re-implementing a base method with the exact same signature (runtime)
Overriding has different return types only
explanation: Overloading provides multiple methods with same name but distinct parameters in one class; overriding redefines a base method in a derived class.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a "Virtual Method Table" (vtable) and "vptr" in C++ runtime implementation?
options: A list of all global variables
A lookup table of function pointers created for classes with virtual functions, with each object storing an invisible pointer (vptr) to its class vtable for dynamic dispatch
explanation: The compiler creates a vtable containing pointers to virtual methods; objects contain a vptr pointing to their class’s vtable to dispatch method calls at runtime.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between Composition and Inheritance ("HAS-A" vs "IS-A" relationship)?
options: Inheritance models an "IS-A" hierarchy (e.g., Dog is an Animal); Composition models a "HAS-A" relationship where a class contains references/instances of other classes (e.g., Car has an Engine)
Composition uses more memory than inheritance
explanation: Software engineering favors composition over inheritance for loose coupling: "HAS-A" delegates tasks, while "IS-A" creates rigid class hierarchies.
subject: Programming Languages

question: In Java, why is Multiple Inheritance of classes disallowed, and how is its behavior supported instead?
options: To avoid memory consumption; supported via packages
To avoid the Diamond Problem and architectural ambiguity; supported by allowing a class to implement multiple Interfaces
Java does not allow inheritance at all
explanation: Java eliminates class-based multiple inheritance to prevent ambiguity, allowing classes to implement multiple interfaces instead.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the purpose of the "super" (or base in C#) keyword in object-oriented languages?
options: To call methods or constructors of the immediate parent (superclass)
explanation: The "super" keyword provides explicit access to overridden methods and constructors of the parent superclass.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the "Liskov Substitution Principle" (LSP) in SOLID design principles?
options: Subclasses should always have more methods than superclasses
Objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of its subclasses without breaking application correctness
Classes should only have one method
explanation: LSP dictates that derived classes must honor the contracts of their base types without altering expected behavior or throwing unexpected exceptions.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the "Single Responsibility Principle" (SRP) in SOLID design?
options: A class should have only one single reason to change (should encapsulate one focused responsibility)
A program should have only one developer
Each function must have only one line of code
explanation: SRP asserts that each class should focus on a single piece of functionality, reducing coupling and making maintenance straightforward.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is an "Interface" in OOP languages like Java or TypeScript?
options: A completely abstract blueprint defining method signatures that conforming classes must implement, containing no instance state
explanation: An interface specifies what a class must do without specifying how it does it, enabling polymorphism across unrelated hierarchies.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a "Static Method" in a class?
options: A method that cannot be run
A method that belongs to the class itself rather than to any specific object instance, callable without instantiating the class
A method that changes its code at runtime
explanation: Static methods operate on the class level and do not have access to an implicit "this" instance reference.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the purpose of a Constructor in a class?
options: To destroy an object when execution ends
A special initialization member function invoked automatically upon object instantiation to set up initial state and allocate resources
explanation: Constructors initialize object fields, allocate necessary resources, and enforce invariants whenever a new class instance is created.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What are the built-in Mutable data types in Python?
explanation: Lists, Dictionaries, and Sets can be altered in-place after creation (mutable). Numbers, Strings, and Tuples are immutable.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the output of the Python expression: [1, 2, 3] * 2?
options: Error: multiplication not supported for lists
explanation: The asterisk operator on Python sequences (lists, strings, tuples) performs sequence repetition: [1, 2, 3] * 2 = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3].
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between "==" and "is" in Python?
options: "==" compares equality of values/contents; "is" tests identity (checks if both variables reference the exact same memory object)
explanation: x == y invokes the __eq__ method to compare data values. x is y checks if id(x) == id(y) (same object identity in memory).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in CPython?
options: A security feature that blocks viruses
A mutex lock in the CPython interpreter that allows only one native thread to execute Python bytecode at a time, restricting CPU-bound multithreading
A lock on file write operations
explanation: The GIL simplifies CPython memory management and reference counting, but limits CPU-bound multi-threading to single-core execution.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a "Generator" in Python, and which keyword produces its values lazily on-demand?
options: A class that compiles code; return keyword
A function that produces an iterator stream using the "yield" keyword, executing lazily without storing all elements in memory
explanation: Generators yield values one at a time via the "yield" keyword, maintaining function execution state across iterations with low memory usage.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a Python "Decorator"?
options: A higher-order function that takes another function as an argument, extends its behavior without modifying its source code, and returns the modified function
A CSS wrapper for web forms
explanation: Decorators wrap functions (using the @decorator syntax) to augment functionality such as logging, authentication, and caching.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the output of the slice expression: "DSSSB_EXAM"[::-1]?
explanation: The slice [start:stop:step] with step = -1 reverses the entire string: "DSSSB_EXAM" reversed is "MAXE_BSSSD".
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between *args and **kwargs in Python function definitions?
options: *args collects arbitrary positional arguments as a Tuple; **kwargs collects arbitrary keyword arguments as a Dictionary
*args is for numbers; **kwargs is for strings
**kwargs is passed by reference; *args by value
explanation: *args unpacks variable non-keyworded arguments into a tuple; **kwargs unpacks keyworded name=value arguments into a dictionary.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the purpose of the __init__ method in a Python class?
options: The object constructor / initializer method invoked automatically when a new instance of the class is created
To delete the object from memory
explanation: __init__ is the initializer method that receives newly instantiated objects as "self" and initializes their instance attributes.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is List Comprehension in Python?
options: A tool that reads lists aloud
A concise, readable syntactic construct to create new lists by applying expressions and filtering predicates over existing iterables
explanation: List comprehensions (e.g., [x**2 for x in nums if x > 0]) provide an expressive, fast alternative to traditional map/filter loops.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the output of: type((1)) and type((1,)) in Python?
explanation: (1) is an integer enclosed in arithmetic parentheses: int. A single-element tuple requires a trailing comma: (1,) is a tuple.
subject: Programming Languages

question: How does Python handle memory management and deallocation of unused objects?
options: Manual free() calls by the programmer
Automatic Reference Counting combined with a Cyclic Garbage Collector (gc module) to detect circular references
explanation: Python uses reference counting to deallocate objects immediately when refcount reaches 0, augmented by generational GC for reference cycles.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the purpose of the "with" statement (Context Manager) in Python (e.g., with open("file.txt") as f)?
options: To guarantee proper resource setup and cleanup (such as automatically closing files or releasing locks) via __enter__ and __exit__ methods
explanation: Context managers encapsulate try...finally patterns, guaranteeing resource closure even if exceptions occur inside the block.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is a "lambda" function in Python?
options: A function that calculates Greek letters
An anonymous, inline single-expression function defined with the "lambda" keyword (e.g., lambda x: x * 2)
A function running in the cloud
explanation: Lambda functions are small, unnamed inline functions restricted to a single expression, frequently used with sort key functions and map/filter.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the output of: print(bool(0), bool([]), bool(""), bool(None)) in Python?
explanation: In Python, zero, empty containers ([], (), {}, set()), empty strings (""), and None are evaluated as "falsy" (False in boolean context).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the Method Resolution Order (MRO) algorithm used in Python 3 for multiple inheritance?
explanation: Python uses the C3 Linearization algorithm to determine a consistent, monotonic Method Resolution Order (accessible via Class.__mro__).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between deepcopy() and copy() in Python’s "copy" module?
options: copy() creates a shallow copy where inner compound objects are referenced; deepcopy() recursively clones all nested objects creating fully independent copies
explanation: Shallow copy (copy.copy) constructs a new collection but inserts references to original child objects; copy.deepcopy copies nested objects recursively.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the pass statement in Python?
options: A null statement that serves as a syntactic placeholder where code is required but no action is to be performed
explanation: "pass" is a no-operation placeholder used when syntax requires a statement (e.g., in empty function stubs or pass-through exception blocks).
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the difference between append() and extend() on a Python list?
options: append() adds its argument as a single element; extend() iterates over its iterable argument and appends each element individually
append() sorts the list; extend() does not
explanation: list.append([4, 5]) appends the sublist as one item: [1, [4, 5]]; list.extend([4, 5]) unrolls elements: [1, 4, 5].
subject: Programming Languages

question: What builtin function returns an iterator of tuples containing the index and item when looping over a sequence?
explanation: enumerate(iterable, start=0) yields (index, value) pairs, allowing clean indexed traversal without manual counter tracking.
subject: Programming Languages

question: What is the fundamental sequential model of the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) where each phase must finish before the next begins?
explanation: The classical Waterfall model is a linear sequential SDLC model comprising Requirement, Design, Implementation, Verification, and Maintenance phases.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is the primary distinctive feature of Boehm’s Spiral Model of software development?
options: Explicit Risk Analysis and risk mitigation at every iteration/quadrant
explanation: The Spiral Model incorporates iterative development with heavy emphasis on early and continuous risk assessment and reduction.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is the difference between Verification and Validation in software engineering?
options: Verification asks: "Are we building the product right?" (reviews, walkthroughs, code inspection); Validation asks: "Are we building the right product?" (testing against user requirements)
Verification is done by clients; validation by coders
Verification requires running code; validation does not
explanation: Verification checks adherence to specifications without code execution; Validation confirms the software satisfies end-user operational needs.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is "Black-Box Testing" (Functional Testing)?
options: Testing hardware in a dark room
Testing software functionality without any knowledge of internal code structure, paths, or implementation details
explanation: Black-box testing focuses strictly on software inputs and expected outputs according to specifications, disregarding internal source code logic.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is "White-Box Testing" (Structural / Glass-Box Testing)?
options: Testing software with complete access to source code, testing branch coverage, condition paths, and internal logic flows
explanation: White-box testing evaluates code execution paths, branches, loops, and conditions based on explicit visibility of the source codebase.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is Boundary Value Analysis (BVA) in software test design?
options: Testing only the middle values of input ranges
A black-box test design technique that tests values at the boundaries of equivalence partitions (min, min+1, nominal, max-1, max)
explanation: BVA targets input boundary conditions because errors in programming logic (e.g., < instead of <=) cluster overwhelmingly at boundaries.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is Equivalence Partitioning (Equivalence Class Partitioning)?
options: Dividing the software codebase into equal-sized files
Dividing input data of software into valid and invalid partitions from which representative test cases are selected, assuming all members behave identically
explanation: Equivalence partitioning partitions input domain into classes where any single test case represents the behavior of all inputs in that partition.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is "Regression Testing"?
options: Re-executing test suites to verify that recent code changes or bug fixes have NOT adversely affected or broken existing functionality
explanation: Regression testing ensures that new features or bug patches do not reintroduce old defects or corrupt previously working modules.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is Cyclomatic Complexity in software metrics (McCabe’s metric)?
options: The number of lines of source code
A quantitative measure of the number of linearly independent paths through a program’s source code module (V(G) = E - N + 2P)
The number of functions in a class
explanation: McCabe’s cyclomatic complexity measures control-flow decision density (V(G) = Edges - Nodes + 2 * Components), indicating the minimum test cases needed for full branch coverage.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is the difference between High Cohesion and Loose Coupling in good software design?
options: High cohesion means elements within a module strongly belong together and serve a single purpose; Loose coupling means modules are minimally dependent on each other
High cohesion means modules call each other constantly
Loose coupling means having no functions
explanation: High Cohesion within modules and Low (Loose) Coupling between modules are hallmarks of modular, robust, and maintainable software architecture.
subject: Software Engineering

question: Which of the following represents the WORST (least desirable) type of coupling between software modules?
options: Content Coupling (one module directly accesses or modifies internal data/code of another)
explanation: Content coupling is the tightest and worst form of coupling: modifications in one module unpredictably break dependent modules.
subject: Software Engineering

question: Which of the following represents the BEST (most desirable) type of cohesion inside a software module?
options: Functional Cohesion (all elements of the module cooperate to execute a single well-defined task)
explanation: Functional cohesion is the ideal cohesion type: every part of the module contributes directly to performing a single, specific function.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is the COCOMO model (Constructive Cost Model) by Barry Boehm used for?
options: Estimating software effort, project cost, and schedule duration based on size in KLOC (Kilo Lines of Code)
explanation: COCOMO calculates development person-months and schedules based on code volume (KLOC) across Organic, Semi-detached, and Embedded project categories.
subject: Software Engineering

question: In Agile Scrum framework, what is a "Sprint"?
options: A time-boxed iteration (typically 1 to 4 weeks) during which the team commits to deliver a potentially shippable product increment
A quick bug patch applied on production servers
A marathon coding session lasting 24 hours
explanation: Sprints are fixed-length iterative development cycles where development items from the Product Backlog are implemented, tested, and demonstrated.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is a "Burn-Down Chart" in Agile project tracking?
options: A graphical representation showing the amount of remaining work (hours or story points) on the vertical axis versus elapsed sprint time on the horizontal axis
A financial report of hardware costs
explanation: Burndown charts track sprint progress, visually comparing the actual velocity slope against the ideal linear trendline toward zero remaining work.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is Alpha Testing versus Beta Testing?
options: Alpha testing is conducted by internal developers/testers at the developer’s site; Beta testing is conducted by actual prospective end-users in their own real operating environments
Alpha is black-box; Beta is white-box
explanation: Alpha testing is performed in-house in a controlled environment; Beta testing collects real-world feedback from target end-users before general release.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is Integration Testing, and what are the two common strategies: Top-Down and Bottom-Up?
options: Testing interfaces between integrated software units; Top-down uses stubs to simulate lower modules, while Bottom-up uses drivers to stimulate higher modules
explanation: Integration testing validates interfaces between combined modules. Top-Down employs dummy stubs; Bottom-Up uses test drivers to invoke lower-level components.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is the difference between a "Stub" and a "Driver" in software integration testing?
options: A Stub replaces a called subordinate module (simulating lower-level response); a Driver replaces a calling module (invoking the module under test from above)
Stubs are hardware; Drivers are software
Drivers test UI; Stubs test databases
explanation: In Top-Down testing, Stubs simulate incomplete downstream modules. In Bottom-Up testing, Drivers act as master modules calling the components under test.
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is Capability Maturity Model Integration (CMMI) Level 5?
options: Optimizing (focus on continuous quantitative process improvement and defect prevention)
explanation: CMMI levels: 1-Initial, 2-Managed, 3-Defined, 4-Quantitatively Managed, 5-Optimizing (continuous process optimization).
subject: Software Engineering

question: What is Mutation Testing in software testing theory?
options: Modifying code randomly until it runs faster
A fault-based testing technique where deliberate minor faults (mutants) are injected into the code to evaluate the adequacy and effectiveness of test suites (killing mutants)
explanation: Mutation testing measures test suite quality by injecting small syntax mutants; a strong test suite detects and fails on all mutated versions ("kills" them).
subject: Software Engineering
